title: The lamp
hookLine: Agni hides; why the lamp is lit first and greeted
carry: the lamp's light is greeted as god
last: THE MURTI IS AN HONORED GUEST.

lines: ONE MATCH, AND THE ROOM CHANGES.
cards: The power goes out at night. The fridge stops humming. Everyone goes quiet.
Somebody fumbles in a drawer, finds a candle, strikes a match. And the whole room changes. Faces come back.
People talk more softly, as if the little flame were listening. Many Hindu homes light a flame on purpose, every evening, even when the power is fine.
It's the second object on the shelf, and it comes with one of the oldest stories in Hinduism.

teach.b: In the oldest hymns, the Rig Veda, fire is a god: Agni, the one who carries every offering up to the gods. And one hymn tells how Agni ran away.
He was afraid of the work; the fires before him, he says, had worn out in that service. So he hid, deep in the waters and the plants, and the offerings had no one to carry them.

The gods went looking, found him, and coaxed him: come back. They promised him a share of the offerings and a life that wouldn't age. And Agni came out and took his place again, between the people and the gods.
That's the flame in a Hindu home.

teach.h: DEEPA — FROM A ROOT: TO SHINE.
teach.b: The Sanskrit word for the lamp is deepa, from a root meaning to shine. Often it's a small clay diya with a cotton wick in ghee or oil, lit at dawn and at dusk, and often lit as puja begins.
Many families greet it with a short verse beginning shubham karoti kalyanam, honoring the lamp's light for bringing what is good and pushing away what harms.
Many go on: deepa jyoti parabrahma, the lamp's light is the supreme Brahman. That's the teaching. The flame isn't only a sign that God is near.

teach.h: THE LAMP'S LIGHT IS GREETED AS GOD.
teach.b: Many Hindus greet the light itself as God, the one reality shining in everything, small enough to sit in a clay bowl. So it's lit first, and bowed to.
And people point out one more thing: when one lamp lights another, it loses nothing. That's why, back on day five, arti was light passed hand to hand.

how: Many Hindu households light a small lamp, often a clay diya with a cotton wick in ghee or oil, at the home shrine at dawn and at dusk, and many greet its light with a short Sanskrit verse beginning shubham karoti kalyanam, often followed by deepa jyoti parabrahma.

o: a festival of lights held each autumn
the red dot worn on the forehead
a small lamp lit at the edges of the day

games.q: what's in the lamp — tap the pairs.
p: the lamp, from a root meaning to shine
fire, who carries offerings to the gods

s: a home lamp has to be an elaborate brass one
a small clay diya, or even a tea light, is how many people do it. the flame is the point.
in a Rig Veda hymn, Agni once hid from his work
he hid in the waters and plants until the gods coaxed him back with a share of the offerings.
the shrine lamp is lit just so you can see the image
many families greet the light itself as God: deepa jyoti parabrahma.

games.q: it's dusk. your grandmother lights the lamp at her shrine and folds her hands to it before she turns on the TV. what is she doing?
o: greeting the light itself as God, as many families do.
making a wish on the flame.
games.why: many families bow to the lit lamp and say a verse: deepa jyoti parabrahma, the lamp's light is Brahman.

practice: If it's safe, light a candle or a lamp somewhere steady, away from anything that can catch; if not, picture one.
Let your eyes rest on the flame softly, without staring hard, and notice how it moves with your breath, the bright middle, the blue at the base.
Then close your eyes for a moment, see if the shape of it stays, and open them: one flame, that's all.

wordCard.voice: Deepa. The lamp: a small flame, from a root meaning to shine, lit at the edges of the day and greeted as God.

orig.note: Sanskrit dīpa: lamp, from the root dīp, to shine or blaze. Deepa and diya are everyday forms.

carryVoice: Your line: the lamp's light is greeted as God. One flame, and it loses nothing when it's shared. Until tomorrow.
